catalog_locator: Grammatik, Kapitel I 'Alphabet und Aussprache', §8 (Betonung), p. 198; context §3 p. 195 and §4 p. 196.
catalog_quote: 8. Bezüglich der Regeln der Betonung muß darauf geachtet werden, ob ein Wort ein zusammengesetztes oder ein einfaches ist. Bei einfachen zwei- und dreisilbigen Wörtern mit allen oder zwei letzten kurzen Silben ruht die Betonung auf der ersten Silbe. Beispiele: kinji, kneifen; ūjaloñ, breit (Insel); jogajok, Moskito. Ist in dreisilbigen Wörtern die zweite Silbe lang, so erhält diese die Betonung: jeūrur, Unruhe, Aufruhr. Übrigens nimmt die letzte Silbe, falls sie lang und die andern kurz sind, die Betonung an: z. B. jeroān, verschwenden, vergeuden; buīn, sein Geruch.

new_statements.translation: 8. As regards the rules of stress, attention must be paid to whether a word is compound or simple. In simple two- and three-syllable words in which all syllables, or the last two, are short, the stress rests on the first syllable. Examples: kinji 'to pinch'; ūjaloñ 'broad (of an island)'; jogajok 'mosquito'. If in three-syllable words the second syllable is long, it receives the stress: jeūrur 'unrest, uproar'. Moreover, the last syllable takes the stress if it is long and the others are short: e.g. jeroān 'to squander, waste'; buīn 'its smell'. (Vowel-length diacritics on the examples are as read from the page image; the scanned text layer drops some of them.)

Bei einfachen zwei- und dreisilbigen Wörtern mit allen oder zwei letzten kurzen Silben ruht die Betonung auf der ersten Silbe. Beispiele: kinji, kneifen; ūjaloñ, breit (Insel); jogajok, Moskito. Ist in dreisilbigen Wörtern die zweite Silbe lang, so erhält diese die Betonung: jeūrur, Unruhe, Aufruhr.…
new_statements.rule_in_words: In simple (underived) words stress falls on the first syllable when the syllables are short; a long syllable (long vowel) attracts the stress, whether it is the second syllable of a trisyllable or the final syllable. weight-sensitive with initial default. The same section adds morphological conditions: prefixes ka- and ri- do not shift stress (jūdak / kajūdak; belle / ribelle); directional suffixes -dok, -lok, -waj leave stress on the stem (bōge / bōgelok); a directional adverb inserted before such a suffix takes the stress (bōkliñlok, wanlāllak); stress often moves to the following syllable when an object pronoun is suffixed to the verb (āadoñ 'to smell' vs. āadoñe 'smell it'); and a prefixed subject pronoun takes the stress (eiet 'they are few', stem iet).
new_statements.exceptions: Compound vs. simple words treated separately; stem stress retained under ka-/ri- prefixation and -dok/-lok/-waj suffixation; a directional adverb before the suffix is stressed; object-pronoun suffixation often shifts stress rightward; a prefixed subject pronoun (e-, en) takes the stress. No claim that stress is contrastive; no minimal pairs given.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rule for simple words, with statements for derived/inflected verb forms; no distinction between citation and connected-speech forms. Note this is a 1906 missionary description in a pre-phonemic orthography whose vowel-length marking is admitted to be uncertain (p. 196 §4: only long vowels are marked); the modern analyses (Bender 1968/1969, Bender-Capelle-Pagotto 2016) could not be opened and may supersede it, e.g. by treating stress as non-distinctive.
new_statements.identity_note: Erdland 1906 describes Marshallese as a whole; the foreword (p. VI) is dated Jaluit (Ralik chain), 12 June 1904, says he worked on several atolls with older speakers, and notes lexical and vowel divergence between the Radak (Ratak) and Rālik groups without assigning his stress rules to either dialect. Ralik-based description is likely but not stated. Glottolog dialect codes for Ralik/Ratak not verified here.

tone_statements.citation: Ng, Sara Blalock. 2017. Phonemic Inventory of Marshallese, and some General Properties. Term paper (dated 15 December 2017), Department of Linguistics, University of Washington. 11 pp. (hosted at linguistics.washington.edu).
tone_statements.quote: Marshallese does not have inflectional or derivational tone. However, changes in pitch and intensity comprise the intonational system of the language. Zewen (1977) notes that while stress in Marshallese is not as distinctive as some languages (e.g. Germanic languages), incorrect stress nevertheless creates ungrammatical structures in the languages. ... Intonation in Marshallese is a combination of pitch and intensity, and is correlated with segmental length (Bender 1969). ... Berbusse and Grama (2011) conducted an intonational analysis of recorded Marshallese using the ToBI labeling scheme.
tone_statements.locator: sec. 4.2 'Intonation and Stress', pp. 7-8: the 'does not have inflectional or derivational tone' sentence and the start of Table 9 on p. 7; rest of Table 9 and the Bender 1969 / Berbusse & Grama sentences on p. 8; Table 10 'Tune Types in Marshallese' on p. 9 (not p. 8)
tone_statements.summary: No lexical tone; intonational tunes only (H* L-L% declarative, H* H-H% polar question).

sources.note: Grammatik Kap. I §8 (p. 198): stress on the first syllable of simple words with short syllables; a long second syllable in trisyllables, or a long final syllable, takes the stress; prefixes ka-/ri- and suffixes -dok/-lok/-waj do not shift stem stress; directional adverbs, object-pronoun suffixes and subject-pronoun prefixes can shift it. Also p. 195 §3: in vowel sequences the unstressed vowel attaches closely to the stressed one; u is rarely stressed.

sources.citation: Hernsheim, Franz. 1880. Beitrag zur Sprache der Marshall-Inseln. Leipzig: Fr. Thiel. 101 pp. (II. Grammatikalischer Leitfaden der Marshall-Sprache, pp. 19-32). Scan: Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, MDZ bsb11646506.
sources.note: No lexical-tone content; German 'Ton' here = word accent. The Leitfaden's sound notes cover the letter inventory, vowels 'sowohl lang als kurz', diphthongs, weak nasals, and an explicit accent rule: disyllabic stems are accented on the first syllable, apparent exceptions (emit, emán) are monosyllabic stems with prefix e-, compounds keep the stem accent, and only compound verbs move the accent to the directional element.

tone.quote: Die Wortstämme sind ein- und zweisylbig, in letzterem Falle liegt der Ton auf der ersten Sylbe: ... denn Worte wie: ... emit todt, fertig ... emán gut sind nicht zwei-, sondern einsylbige Stämme mit dem Präfix e; auch bei zusammengesetzten Wörtern bleibt der Ton wie im Stamme: bógedok herbringen (bóge nehmen), ... Nur bei zusammengesetzten Zeitwörtern geht der Ton auf die Sylbe über, welche die wichtigste Richtung ausdrückt: wanlíngelok hinaufgehen, anginláldok herabführen.
tone.translation: Word stems are mono- and disyllabic; in the latter case the accent lies on the first syllable: ... for words like ... emit 'dead, finished' ... emán 'good' are not disyllabic but monosyllabic stems with the prefix e; in compound words too the accent stays as in the stem: bógedok 'bring here' (bóge 'take'), ... Only in compound verbs does the accent pass to the syllable that expresses the most important direction: wanlíngelok 'go up', anginláldok 'lead down'.

sources.citation: Matsuoka, Shizuo (松岡静雄). 1929. マーシャル語の研究 (Maasharu-go no kenkyuu) [A study of the Marshallese language]. Tokyo: Kyodo Kenkyusha (郷土研究社). Ch. 1 '音' (sounds), sec. 3 '抑揚' pp. 22-23. National Diet Library Digital Collections pid 1126875.
sources.note: The suprasegmental section (抑揚 'rise and fall') describes word prosody as a single raised syllable (揚音), as a rule the word-initial one, with the end of the word lowered; the raised syllable is lengthened or geminated; the pattern survives compounding, prefixes ka-, ri- and suffixes -tok, -lok, -waj do not change it, and rarely suffixation puts the raise on the second syllable. This is a culminative accent described in pitch terms (matching Hernsheim 1880/Erdland 1906 initial stress), not a claim of lexical tone contrast.

tone.quote: 三、抑揚 マーシャル語は次章に述べるやうに大部分は結合語で、比較的少數なる原語、即ち純粹の單語は多くは二語音以下を以て構成せられて居る。此等の原語に抑揚を施す必要がある場合には多くは語頭を揚げ、語尾を抑へることを例とするものゝやうで、強められた語音が長韻又は促音となるのは當然の結果である。此抑揚は他語(又は語分子)と結合した場合にも存續するのが普通であるから、語の構成を明にすれば揚音の所在を知ることもさのみ困難ではないが、時としては結合(又は接合)分子に揚音が移り或は抑揚のない語が結合の爲に新に之を得ることがある。
tone.translation: 3. Rise and fall (accent). As stated in the next chapter, Marshallese words are for the most part compounds; the comparatively few primitive words, i.e. pure simple words, mostly consist of two syllables or fewer. When such primitive words have to be given a rise-and-fall, the rule seems to be that the beginning of the word is raised and the end of the word lowered, and it is a natural consequence that the strengthened syllable becomes a long vowel or a geminate. This modulation normally persists when the word is combined with other words (or word-elements), so that once the make-up of a word is clear it is not very hard to know where the raised syllable lies; but at times the raised syllable moves onto the combined (or attached) element, or a word that had no modulation newly acquires one through combination.
tone.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone.summary: One raised (high, lengthened) syllable per word, normally word-initial; accentual, no lexical tone contrast described.
